_: Source for the hands-on lab. Edit this, then run npm run sync. Template and snippet text are arrays of lines. Step details (everything except id, lesson, title, sections, minutes) are encrypted with the lesson for paid lessons.

sections.title: Project header
template: | **System** | _One sentence: what it is, and who it is for_ |

sections.title: 1. Introduction and Goals
template: _One paragraph: what the system replaces and why. No technology names. Then 3 to 5 key functions._

sections.title: 2. Constraints
template: | C1 | _what is imposed_ | _who or what imposes it_ | _what it rules out_ |

sections.title: 3. Context and Scope
template: | Neighbour | Protocol or format | Direction | What goes wrong |

sections.title: 4. Solution Strategy
template: | #goal | _specific approach_ | _reason, cite a constraint_ | _what you accept_ |

sections.title: 5. Building Block View
template: - _what must be true before the call_

sections.title: 6. Runtime View
template: ### 6.1 _Verb the flow, e.g. Place and pay for an order_

sections.title: 7. Deployment View
template: | Node or service | Runs | Fails how / noticed how |
_Production, test, dev. Then the pipeline in 4 or 5 boxes._

sections.title: 8. Crosscutting Concepts
template: **_Concept name_.** _Rule. Where it applies. Why. Link to an ADR or scenario._

snippets.label: Concept
text: **_Concept name_.** _Rule. Where it applies. Why. Link (ADR-0001 or Q1)._

sections.title: 10. Quality Requirements
template: | Q1 | #goal | _what happens_ | _what the system does_ | _a number_ |

sections.title: 11. Risks and Technical Debt
template: | ID | Risk or debt | Mitigation or payback | Owner |

sections.title: AGENTS.md (agent index)
template: - Rules: _three or four, each with the thing to do instead_
- Check: _the command that verifies the rules_

sections.title: Working notes (not part of arc42)
template: | 1 | _quote from the AI answer_ | _spec / align / verify_ | _red / orange / yellow_ | _accepted / rejected / edited_ | _reason_ |

steps.title: Set up your project
steps.brief: This is where your arc42 lives for the whole course. Nothing to copy or paste: the skeleton is already here.
do: Type your system's name in the box at the top. Pick one your team could explain from memory.
In the project header, replace the placeholder with one sentence: what the system is and who it is for.
Write three likely users.
Read what you wrote once. Remove anything confidential.
done: The system has a name
The purpose is one sentence
Three users are named
No passwords, keys, personal data or client material
steps.experienced: Choose the system whose missing documentation would hurt most if its main developer left tomorrow.

steps.title: Team table and first diagram
steps.brief: A warm-up for the two things you will write most: tables and diagrams.
do: Use the Team table button to add a three-row table of names and roles.
Use the Mermaid graph button to insert a graph. Change it to draw You, Your phone, Messaging app, with one labelled arrow.
Open the diagram in the Mermaid Live editor from the preview, and confirm it draws without errors.
done: The team table has three rows
The diagram has one labelled arrow
Both render without errors
steps.experienced: Add a sequence diagram of one real flow from your own system.

steps.title: Write section 1: goals
steps.brief: Exercise 1 from the live day. One page that says why the system exists and what must be true of it.
do: 1.1 (5 min): one paragraph on what the system replaces, with no technology names, then three to five key functions.
1.3 (8 min): five or six stakeholders, each with an expectation of the architecture.
1.2 (12 min): your top three quality goals, each with one short scenario in section 10 form, with a number in it.
done: 1.1 says what the system replaces and names no technology
There are 3 to 5 quality goals, none of them a project goal
Every goal has a scenario with a number
Every stakeholder has an expectation
Each goal traces to a stakeholder
steps.experienced: Draft all three parts for a real system first. Then compare with the worked example.

steps.title: Write section 2: constraints
steps.brief: Exercise 2. What is imposed on you from outside, so you do not spend design effort on it.
do: Write four to six numbered constraints, covering at least three kinds (technical, organisational, legal or convention).
For each, fill in why it exists and its effect on the design.
Apply the three-question test from the lesson to each row. Delete or rewrite any that fail.
done: 4 to 6 constraints, each with an ID
At least three different kinds
Every row has a why and an effect
Each passes the three-question test
steps.experienced: Find one constraint your team treats as fixed that is really negotiable.

steps.title: Write section 3: context
steps.brief: Exercise 3. The system as a black box, and everything that talks to it.
do: List the neighbours silently first: people, other systems, and things that happen on a schedule.
Edit the diagram in 3.1: one box for your system, one box per neighbour, every arrow labelled.
Fill the technical table in 3.2: protocol or format and direction for each neighbour.
done: Every arrow is labelled
No internal parts appear
People and time-based neighbours are included
Direction is shown for each exchange
steps.experienced: Add a failure-behaviour entry for your three riskiest interfaces.

steps.title: Write section 4: strategy
steps.brief: Exercise 4. For each quality goal, the approach you chose and what you give up.
do: Copy your three quality goals from section 1.2.
For each: brainstorm two approaches, choose one, and say why, citing a constraint if relevant.
State the trade-off you accept. Check that no constraint forbids the approach.
Test it: could a neighbour read only this table and guess two things about your architecture? If not, make it more specific.
done: One row per quality goal
Each approach is specific, not generic
Each row names a trade-off
No approach breaks a constraint
steps.experienced: For each row, name the strongest alternative you rejected.

steps.title: Write section 5: building blocks
steps.brief: Exercises 5a and 5b. The parts of your system, and one precise contract for the riskiest part.
do: List the responsibilities from 1.1, group the related ones, and name each group with a noun, not a technology.
Draw the Level 1 diagram with labelled uses-arrows, and fill the block table with one sentence of responsibility each.
Check the count (5 to 9) and check each block against section 4 or a quality goal.
Pick your riskiest block and its most important operation. Write pre-conditions, post-conditions, invariants and error modes.
done: 5 to 9 blocks, no brand names
Every block has one responsibility sentence
The diagram and the table use identical names
The contract gives the caller a visible result for every error
A stranger could write a test from the contract
steps.experienced: Add a reason-to-change column and justify one split by it. Then write one invariant as a test in your own stack.

steps.title: Write section 6: runtime
steps.brief: Exercise 6. One important flow, step by step, with the failure branch.
do: Name the scenario with a verb, such as Place and pay for an order.
List the participants: only blocks from section 5 and neighbours from section 3.
Write the steps in plain words, then turn them into messages in the sequence diagram, eight steps or fewer.
Add one failure branch, and a three-line caption on what to notice.
done: Participant names match section 5 exactly
There is a failure branch with a visible outcome
There is a caption that says what to notice
Eight steps or fewer
steps.experienced: Document the failure scenario most likely to wake someone at night instead.

steps.title: Write section 7: deployment
steps.brief: Exercise 7. Where each block runs, and what you do not control.
do: List your environments: production, test, dev.
For production, list the nodes or services and map every section 5 block to one.
Note anything outside your control, such as a SaaS provider.
Describe the pipeline in four or five boxes.
done: Every block appears in the mapping table
Outside dependencies are named
The pipeline is described
steps.experienced: Add one line per node: how it fails and how you would notice.

steps.title: Write section 8: concepts
steps.brief: Exercise 8. Ideas that recur across several blocks, written once.
do: Find three recurring ideas across your blocks (for example error handling, identity, time).
Write each as one paragraph: name, rule, where it applies, why, and a link to an ADR or scenario.
Name the pattern. Do not write a tutorial.
done: Three concepts
Each states a rule
Each says where it applies
Each links to an ADR or scenario
steps.experienced: Pick the concept most often violated in your real code and write the rule so it could be linted.

steps.title: Write section 9: one decision
steps.brief: Exercise 9. One significant decision, recorded so a newcomer understands why not the other option.
do: Pick one significant decision your architecture depends on.
Write the context in two or three sentences, and at least two real options.
State the decision and the main reason.
List consequences: at least one good and at least one bad. Link to the goal or constraint it serves, and set status and date.
done: Two real options, not a straw man
A bad consequence that actually stings
Linked to a goal or constraint
One decision only
steps.experienced: Write the ADR for a decision your team made without one, and see whether you still agree.

steps.title: Write section 10: scenarios
steps.brief: Exercise 10. Make the quality requirements testable.
do: Add the quality tree in 10.1: qualities, with your goals as leaves.
Add one change scenario and one failure scenario in 10.2.
Give each a measurable number and a link to a quality goal.
done: Every scenario has a number
Every leaf links to a goal
Usage, change and failure are all represented
steps.experienced: Add the scenario your current system is most likely to fail.

steps.title: Write sections 11 and 12
steps.brief: Exercise 11. What could go wrong, and the words you use.
do: Add two risks, each with a mitigation and an owner.
Add five glossary terms that a newcomer would get wrong.
Check that every risk or debt ID is referenced somewhere else in the document.
done: Two risks with mitigation and owner
Five glossary terms
IDs are used elsewhere in the document
steps.experienced: Add the technical debt your team accepted last quarter, with the payback condition.

steps.title: Red-team your draft with AI
steps.brief: The AI lab. Use any AI assistant outside this site on your own draft, then log what you found here.
do: Use Download arc42.md, or copy the full document. Remove anything confidential before you paste it anywhere.

In your AI assistant: ask it to act as a software architect and, using your draft as the source of truth, produce a critique and proposed fixes. Keep its full answer, including its assumptions and questions.
Red-team it: find at least five flaws. In the Working notes flaw log, quote each one, tag the lens (specification, misalignment, verification) and a severity.
Repair: mark every AI line Accepted, Rejected or Edited, with a reason. Apply the accepted fixes to your own sections.
done: Nothing confidential was pasted
At least five flaws are logged
Every logged flaw has a verdict and a reason
Accepted fixes are applied in your sections
steps.experienced: Ask the assistant to list every claim that your draft does not support.

steps.title: Write an agent index
steps.brief: Write for two readers: people, and coding agents. A short index beats a long document.
do: Replace the placeholders: one line on what the system is, and pointers to your arc42 sections.
Write three or four rules, each with what to do instead of the forbidden thing.
Name the check that would catch a broken rule.
Keep it short enough to read in a minute.
done: Under about 150 lines, and much shorter at first
Every rule says what to do instead
It points to the document instead of copying it
A check is named for each rule
steps.experienced: Turn one invariant from your contract into a test case written in your own stack.

steps.title: Assemble and check
steps.brief: The last step. Run the health check, fix what it finds, and take your document with you.
do: Open the Health check. Fix what you can in a few minutes; rough is fine, empty is not.
Read through the Whole document once, top to bottom.
Download arc42.md and put it in your repository this week.
Write the one thing you will do on Monday.
done: All 12 headings are present, even rough
Every quality goal has a scenario with a number
Every section 5 block traces to a strategy or goal
Section 6 participants match section 5 names
At least one ADR with an alternative and a negative consequence
IDs such as C1 and ADR-0001 are referenced at least once elsewhere
steps.experienced: Run the same document through the AI lab again and compare the flaws it finds now.
